body.statement: Let \(M_{\delta}=\mathbf 1\{|Z|>\delta\}\), and suppose \(P(M_{\delta}=1\mid X)<1\) almost surely for every \(\delta>0\), so thresholds with empty mover events are harmless. This baseline-conditional support condition parallels Assumption 5 in de Chaisemartin et al. (arXiv:2201.06898v1, Section 4.1). Under compatibility, the declared continuous support version of \(g\), and parallel trends on \(X_0\), it implies \(\mathcal C_P=\{x\mapsto g(x,0)\}\), \(R(P)=0\), and \(\Theta(P)=\{[T-\int g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x)]/A\}\). This weighted WAOSS singleton recovers the quasi-stayer-limit formula in Theorem 1 of de Chaisemartin, D'Haultf\oe{}uille, and Vazquez-Bare (2024) under the stronger baseline-conditional support condition. Theorem 3 of arXiv:2201.06898v1 is an analogous conditional-support result for the unweighted switcher-slope target \(\delta_1\); this proposition does not claim to nest that estimand. Failure of baseline-conditional support on a set of baseline values having positive \(P\)-probability can yield \(R(P)>0\) and a non-singleton \(\Theta(P)\).
body.justification: The nested corollary separates the proceedings paper's weighted WAOSS formula from the earlier manuscript's analogous unweighted \(\delta_1\) result and locates the new partial-identification region.
body.gap: The proceedings paper gives the weighted WAOSS quasi-stayer formula, while arXiv:2201.06898v1 Assumption 5 and Theorem 3 concern a conditional-support route to the distinct unweighted switcher-slope target \(\delta_1\). Neither gives the sharp weighted WAOSS set when baseline-conditional support fails.
body.consumer: Researchers can use one support diagnostic to decide whether to report the published singleton formula or the sharp obstacle interval.
body.proof_tex:
For each positive integer \(k\), choose a regular conditional probability and write
\[
q_k(x)=P(|Z|\le 1/k\mid X=x).
\]
Since \(M_{1/k}=\mathbf 1\{|Z|>1/k\}\), the assumed inequality \(P(M_{1/k}=1\mid X)<1\) says that \(q_k(X)>0\) almost surely.  Fix \(x\in X_0\) and let \(U_k=(x-1/k,x+1/k)\).  By the definition of \(X_0=\operatorname{supp}_P(X)\),
\[
P(X\in U_k)>0.
\]
Because \(q_k>0\) for \(P_X\)-almost every baseline,
\[
P(X\in U_k,|Z|\le1/k)
=\int_{U_k}q_k(x')\,dP_X(x')>0.
\]
A positive-probability Borel set must meet the support \(H=\operatorname{supp}_P(X,Z)\).  Hence there is \((x_k,z_k)\in H\) with \(|x_k-x|<1/k\) and \(|z_k|\le1/k\).  Thus \((x_k,z_k)\to(x,0)\).  Since \(H\) is closed, it follows that
\[
(x,0)\in H\qquad\text{for every }x\in X_0.
\]
This argument uses only support neighborhoods and does not condition on a null singleton.

Under the compatibility clause in the proposition, at least one legal completion exists.  The full-law sharpness theorem then implies \(\mathcal C_P\ne\varnothing\).  For any \(u\in\mathcal C_P\), the support-cone inequality at \((x,0)\) gives
\[
|g(x,0)-u(x)|\le K|0|=0
\qquad(x\in X_0).
\]
Therefore every feasible function equals \(g(\cdot,0)\).  Nonemptiness shows that this function itself is feasible, so
\[
\mathcal C_P=\{x\mapsto g(x,0)\}.
\]
The frontier definitions consequently give
\[
V_P^-=V_P^+=\int_{X_0}g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x),
\qquad
R(P)=0.
\]
Substitution into the attained sharp interval yields
\[
\Theta(P)=
\left\{\frac{T-\int_{X_0}g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x)}{A}\right\}.
\]
This is the weighted WAOSS quasi-stayer-limit formula in Theorem 1 of de Chaisemartin, D'Haultf\oe{}uille, and Vazquez-Bare (2024).  The comparison with Assumption 5 and Theorem 3 of arXiv:2201.06898v1 is only an analogy in the support condition: that theorem concerns the distinct unweighted target \(\delta_1\), and no equality of estimands is used here.

Finally, the already established source-class recession-ray proposition supplies the declared continuous law \(P^{\circ}\).  At that law, baseline-conditional zero support fails on a set of \(P_X^{\circ}\)-probability \(p_{\circ}>0\), while the bounded sensitivity class has
\[
\Theta(P^{\circ})=
\left[-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
       \frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}}\right].
\]
The interval is nondegenerate, so the point-identification proposition implies \(R(P^{\circ})>0\).  This proves the stated possibility claim; it does not assert that every failure of conditional support is sufficient for \(R(P)>0\).
